[A correct diagram of the functioning part of a galvanometer, correctly labelled is sufficient
for a student to gain the full three marks available for this question.] The key part of a
galvanometer is a coil within an external magnetic field with curved pole-pieces. If a current
passes through the coil, it will rotate within the external field — a consequence of the motor
effect. A needle attached to the coil moves across a scale, allowing the amount of current to
be measured. A coiled spring is attached to the coil, to provide a counter-torque on the coil,
allowing the scale to be calibrated, and to force the coil back to zero when no current flows
through the coil. Curved pole-pieces of the permanent magnet produce a radial magnetic field
around the coil to eliminate the ‘cos factor, so the scale can be uniform.
